You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

What was the outcome of this study?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	**Weight gain among US adults during the COVID‐19 pandemic**
     2	
     3	Although the COVID‐19 pandemic and the subsequent mitigation strategies have had a significant
     4	impact on the lives and behaviors of many individuals, the effects of the pandemic on weight gain
     5	among adults in the United States are uncertain. A widely publicized study [1] reported a 0.7‐kg
     6	increase in weight per month (February through June 2020), which would equal 18.5 lb if extrapolated
     7	to 12 months, but these findings were based on 269 participants with a Bluetooth‐connected scale. A
     8	meta‐analysis [2] of 35 cross‐sectional studies and 1 cohort study among adults and older
     9	adolescents in various countries found an average 1.6‐kg increase in (self‐reported) weight from
    10	March to May 2020. An American Psychological Association press release [3] in March 2021 also
    11	indicated that among the 42% of adults who reported that they had gained weight during the pandemic,
    12	the mean weight increase was 29 lb (13 kg).
    13	
    14	Other studies have indicated that pandemic‐related weight increases may be smaller than suggested by
    15	these reports. A longitudinal study without formal peer review, based on the electronic health
    16	records (EHR) of about 15 million adults in the United States, for example, concluded that the mean
    17	weight gain during the 12 months of the pandemic (through March 2021) was less than 0.5 kg [4]; this
    18	increase was similar to the annual increase before the pandemic. In addition, a large study of
    19	self‐reported, longitudinal data among adults in the United Kingdom found no change in mean weight
    20	after February 2020 [5].
    21	
    22	Studies among children and adolescents may also be relevant, and four studies [6, 7, 8, 9] have
    23	found that BMI increases were larger during the pandemic than in previous years. For example, Lange
    24	et al. [7] reported that the rate of BMI increase was 0.05 kg/m2 per month before the pandemic and
    25	0.1 kg/m2 per month during the pandemic. These increases, however, were most pronounced among 6‐ to
    26	11‐year‐olds, with 18‐ to 20‐year‐olds showing a smaller increase in BMI during the pandemic than
    27	before the pandemic. Somewhat similar age interactions have been seen by others [6, 8]. Although
    28	increases in the prevalence of obesity were also reported in cross‐sectional analyses [9], this
    29	result may have been influenced by an ascertainment bias [10] because heavier children and
    30	adolescents may have been more likely to be examined during the pandemic.
    31	
    32	It has been suggested that further studies are needed to assess potential group‐specific impacts of
    33	the COVID‐19 epidemic on body weight [2]. Therefore, we examine changes in weight among 18‐ to
    34	84‐year‐olds from January 2019 through May 2021 among 4.24 million adults in a large EHR database to
    35	determine whether weight gain increased during the pandemic. We focus on differences in weight gain
    36	from January 2019 to February 2020 with those after March 2020.
    37	
    38	Data were obtained from IQVIA's Ambulatory Electronic Medical Records database (Version Q3, May 2021
    39	data release), containing deidentified information recorded during outpatient encounters for a
    40	geographically diverse US patient population. This database contains the clinical data of
    41	approximately 80 million patients from January 2006 through May 2021 from all 50 states recorded by
    42	more than 100,000 providers affiliated with over 800 ambulatory large practices and physician
    43	networks. The data set contains key clinical variables, including laboratory values, patient vitals,
    44	health behaviors, diagnoses, and procedures. All data were extracted using the E360
    45	Software‐as‐a‐Service Platform [11].
    46	
    47	The extracted data comprises 43.7 million adults with weight and height measurements from 2009
    48	through 2021. Overall, there are 360 million recorded weights and 297 million heights among these
    49	participants. We calculated age at the examination as the difference between the examination date
    50	and year of birth. To preserve confidentiality, years of birth before 1936 were re‐coded by IQVIA as
    51	1936 so that the maximum age in 2021 would be 85 years. As the 1936 birth year contains several
    52	actual years of birth (e.g., 1936, 1935, 1934), we included only participants born in 1937 or later.
    53	The maximum age in the current study in 2021 is therefore 84 years.
    54	
    55	These data were cleaned using the growthcleanr algorithm for adult data developed to accompany the
    56	growthcleanr pediatric algorithm [12, 13] used in previous studies [7, 14, 15]. This algorithm is
    57	designed to clean clinically obtained longitudinal weights and heights in EHR databases [16]. Many
    58	steps in both the pediatric and adult algorithms are similar and they rely on the deviation of a
    59	value from an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) of a participant's other weights and
    60	heights.
    61	
    62	There are, however, several differences between adult and pediatric algorithms. Although the EWMA in
    63	the pediatric algorithm uses SD scores to account for the expected changes in weight and height with
    64	sex and age, the adult algorithm uses the actual weight and height values. The height algorithm for
    65	adults differs from the children's algorithm because little change is expected among adults.
    66	Furthermore, most repeated values are retained in the adult data but are coded as “carried forwards”
    67	in the pediatric algorithm.
    68	
    69	Of the 360 million weights, 2.1% were excluded based on the growthcleanr algorithm. The largest
    70	exclusion categories were (a) identical same day (0.9%), (b) different values on same day (0.7%),
    71	(c) biologically implausible (0.2%), and (d) EWMA (0.2%). About 2.9% of the 297 million heights were
    72	excluded, with the largest categories being (1) heights of a participant that differed by more than
    73	2 inches (1.3%), (2) identical same day (1.1%), and (3) different values on the same day (0.3%). The
    74	adult algorithm limits the weight range from 20 to 500 kg and the height range from 50 to 244 cm.
    75	
    76	We restricted the analyses to the 16.1 million people examined after January 1, 2019, who were at
    77	least 18 years of age at their first examination. We also required participants to have (1) two or
    78	more visits in the pre‐pandemic period (January 1, 2019, through February 28, 2020) and (2) one or
    79	more visits after June 1, 2020. We chose the latter date as there was an approximately 50% decrease
    80	in the number of examinations conducted in the first few months of the pandemic, which could
    81	introduce a selection bias. For participants with more than one weight or height measurement in a
    82	given month, we selected one value at random. These criteria reduced the sample to 4.25 million
    83	participants with 30.1 million examinations. For weights (14%) without a recorded height on the same
    84	day, we used the median height of the participant (based on all height measurements) to calculate
    85	BMI.
    86	
    87	The median number of visits in this sample was three in the pre‐pandemic period and two in the
    88	postpandemic period. Information on race and ethnicity was optionally reported in a single composite
    89	variable in the database. About 75% of the sample was White, and 8% was Black, but race/ethnicity
    90	was unknown for about 12% of the sample, and < 1% of the participants indicated that they were
    91	Hispanic. As the collection of race/ethnicity data in EHR can be inaccurate [17], we do not focus on
    92	this characteristic.
    93

94	All analyses were performed in R.4.1.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing), and they are based
    95	on 4,246,001 participants examined from January 2019 through May 2021. After showing descriptive
    96	characteristics of the participants at their first and last examinations, we examined the mean
    97	monthly weights in 2020 and 2021 relative to those in 2019. These differences were calculated as the
    98	mean monthly weights in 2020 and 2021 minus the mean weight in the same month in 2019. Because the
    99	number of monthly examinations substantially decreased in April and May 2020, we also examined the
   100	possibility of a selection bias. This sensitivity analysis was limited to the 1 million 18‐ Compared
   101	with the pre‐pandemic weight trend, there was a small increase (0.1 kg) in weight in the first year
   102	of the pandemic (March 2020 through March 2021). Weight changes during the pandemic varied by sex,
   103	age, and initial BMI, but the largest mean increase across these characteristics was < 1.3 kg.
   104	Weight increases were generally greatest among women, adults with BMI of 30 or 35 kg/m2, and younger
   105	adults.to 59‐year‐olds examined in April and May 2019. We contrasted the mean 2019 weights between
   106	those reexamined in April and May 2020 (26%) and those not reexamined (74%).
   107	
   108	We then used mixed‐effects models [18, 19], which use all of the intercorrelated, serial data from a
   109	person, to examine the difference in the rate of weight change between the pre‐pandemic (before
   110	March 2020) and pandemic (after March 2020) periods in the cohort. These sex‐specific models
   111	included a random‐intercepts term to account for individual‐level heterogeneity, initial BMI,
   112	initial age, time (in years) relative to March 1, 2020, and pandemic period. The difference in the
   113	rate of weight change during the pandemic was assessed using an interaction term between the
   114	pandemic period (coded as 0 or 1) and time relative to March 1, 2020. These models allowed the
   115	weight change between the two periods to vary by sex, age, and BMI. We modeled BMI and age using
   116	natural splines [20] to account for nonlinearity.
   117	
   118	The results of these models are displayed graphically for various combinations of sex, initial age
   119	(25, 40, 60, and 75 years), and initial BMI (25, 30, and 35 kg/m2). We also summarize the
   120	differences calculated from this model between the pre‐pandemic and pandemic changes in weight over
   121	1 year. We refer to the difference in weight change during the pandemic and the weight change before
   122	the pandemic from these models as the excess weight gain during the pandemic. This is the weight
   123	gain during the pandemic in excess of that predicted by the pre‐pandemic trend in weight.
   124
